content.text: At the end of the year, the bookstore is busy with inventory, new books being stocked, and old books being organized—it’s a whirlwind of activity. Just now, I arranged this bouquet of flowers, and only at moments like these can my breathing slow down. It reminds me of what you mentioned last time when we were discussing "A Lifelong Journey"—the way to resist the restlessness of the times by focusing on the details.

Seeing your flowers reminds me of the tranquility I felt while organizing artifacts in the museum storeroom. That sense of being alone with time feels very similar. Just like when I shared my grandfather's copper lock last time, the quiet feeling of touching the traces of time always allows one to step away from the busyness of daily life.

Yes, just like when we were making green rice cakes before, focusing on the handmade process kept worries at bay. What's the atmosphere like in your warehouse? I remember you shared the health records of old tea before—does that state of careful observation have something in common with organizing artifacts?

Just like this, the artifacts stand quietly on display, appearing solemn under the light. Each time I arrange them, it feels like reading a silent piece of history. It reminds me of what you mentioned during our discussion about indigo-dyed tea sets—the patience required for hand-dyeing, which must be adjusted according to the weather. Working in the storage room demands a similar kind of slowness and stillness.

This sense of quiet is truly wonderful. Sometimes, when I organize old books in a corner of the bookstore and feel the texture of the pages, it helps calm my mind. Just like how Mo Dian only loves curling up on the pile of old books by the windowsill—that stubborn companionship reminds me to slow down. You once said that old tea only sleeps in the old rattan chair. The quirky habits of pets are really so similar.

Well, physical memories always have this kind of power. Like Grandpa's copper lock or the health records of old tea leaves—when you focus on the details, the flow of time seems to change. It reminds me of when we first discussed making Qingtuan, and you said, "The warmth of paper always makes people slow down and read carefully." Now I feel that any hands-on craft or organizing task that requires focus has this healing effect, much like the "warmth of paper."

Yes, the outside world is accelerating, but these activities slow us down. You mentioned strolling through old neighborhoods earlier—what exactly is that experience like? Is it like observing with an 'archaeological discovery' mindset, similar to how we studied the basket-weaving techniques in *A Lifelong Journey*?

I often visit this old street, observing the architectural details and listening to the sounds of the city. The bricks, tiles, and lanterns all bear the marks of time, and strolling through it, my heart naturally quiets down. It reminds me of the "slow simmering" you mentioned when we discussed eating according to the seasons—like the silver ear and snow pear soup you made. Wandering is also a kind of "slow simmering" of space, allowing memories and perceptions to seep in gradually.

This reminds me of our discussions about *A Lifelong Journey* and the meticulous research into the details of that era. Observing old streets—isn't it like examining life itself? Just as you previously documented the folk differences in qingtuan, now you're extending the focus of your research from food and objects to entire life scenes.

Yes, it connects to the continuity of history. Just like making green rice cakes or hosting a blue-dyed tea ceremony, traditional rhythms can regulate the health of the mind. From spring green rice cakes to autumn and winter dietary supplements, and now to mindful activities, we have been exploring different facets of this 'slow-paced life.' I remember you once said that arranging meals according to the solar terms is like 'writing prose poetry for life.' I feel that activities like strolling, flower arranging, and calligraphy are all different stanzas of that poem.

When it comes to health, I often make snow fungus and pear soup now, following the autumn and winter food therapy list you shared earlier. The slow simmering process is also a way to calm the mind. It reminds me of how we divided tasks when making Qingtuan—I was in charge of the savory filling, and you handled the sweet one. Now, even though we each have our own mindful activities, sharing them feels like a spiritual "exchange of tastes."

That's great. Slow living is not only about diet but also about daily activities. For example, the process of grinding ink itself helps to settle one's mind. This reminds me of the meticulous way I recorded the "texture" of Old Tea's behavior in its health diary—paying attention to the "texture" of brushstrokes during calligraphy practice is also a form of careful observation of the present state.

I've recently taken up calligraphy, and I find that focusing on the lifting, pressing, and turning of the brushstrokes truly helps counteract the restlessness of the outside world. It's more effective than simply resting. Just like how we once admired the hand-hammered marks on the indigo-dyed tea mat, that vitality within the "imperfection" can also be found in calligraphy—every tremor or hesitation in a stroke is a genuine record of one's state of mind in that moment.

Calligraphy is a wonderful practice. Like flower arranging and leisurely walks, it extends well-being from the body to the soul. We can share more of such activities. Starting from the memories of Qingtuan in Session 1, to old objects, handicrafts, pets, films, and now to mindful activities, our conversations have continuously deepened our understanding of "inheritance and preservation"—preserving not just objects, but also the rhythm of life that brings peace to the soul.

Yes, just like when we exchange green rice cakes on weekends, we can chat about our respective methods of finding inner peace. Integrating cultural significance into our adjustments makes life more fulfilling. From the initial 'Search for the Taste of Spring in Green Rice Cakes' to the current 'Mindfulness Activities as a Remedy,' it feels like our conversation has completed a beautiful cycle—from specific food memories to a universal aesthetic of life.

Well, from old objects to handicrafts, and then to these activities, we have always been guarding this rhythm. The end of the year is busy, but there are always ways to find peace. Just like what you said when you shared the indigo-dyed tea ceremony last time, 'supporting a way of life'—now these mindfulness activities are our active shaping and guarding of our own lifestyle.

Thank you for sharing. Next time I stroll through the old district, I'll bring my camera to capture those details, and perhaps I can write a short piece about them. Just like how you wrote a story for your grandfather's copper lock, allowing tangible memories to be 're-presented' through words. From green rice cakes to copper locks, and even the bricks and tiles of the old streets, every discovery is worth recording and sharing.

Looking forward to reading it. A healthy mind requires these specific and actionable adjustments, just as history needs tangible forms to be passed down. From the Qingtuan conversation in March to now in December, every one of our discussions over these past months has been practicing this sense of time—'living between the present and the past.' Mindfulness activities are the perfect remedy for grounding this sense of time in everyday life.
